actions.reason: RegexTokenizer.train used to push a new heap entry for every pair whose count changed, including all the pairs whose count only went down. Those entries were mostly popped later and discarded as stale. Now only pairs whose count goes up get pushed; these are exactly the new pairs that contain idx. A stale entry whose count went down is re-filed with its current count when it reaches the top of the heap, the same scheme pop_top_pairs already uses. Because every pair always has a heap entry at least as large as its current count, the top count and the full set of tied pairs come out the same, so merges and tie-breaks are unchanged. A count that drops to 0 can never rise again, since new pairs always contain the fresh idx. So zero entries stay in stats and are skipped, which removes the per-merge touched list, its set() and the zero-count deletion pass. The error raised when no pairs are left is kept as max over the positive counts. Outputs are identical; train_ir ratio 0.9853.

journal.text:
I worked on RegexTokenizer.train in minbpe/regex.py to cut train_ir. The heap was getting a new entry for every pair whose count changed, including the many whose count only dropped, and most of those were popped later as stale. I changed it so only pairs whose count rises get pushed, which are the new pairs containing idx. A stale entry whose count fell is re-filed with its current count when it reaches the top.

My first attempt changed 16 lines and was rejected: train_ir went from 345049830 to 344076471, ratio 0.9972 against the required 0.9900. Outputs were identical. The fuller version with 53 changed lines was accepted in my sandbox, with train_ir going from 345049830 to 339972090 (ratio 0.9853) and encode_ir at ratio 1.0005. I submitted it and it is queued for replay.

I believe heap churn from decremented pairs is a real cost in training, but the gain is small.

Next I want to look at the per-merge pair count updates themselves, not just the heap traffic.
